prompt: Identify this foundational charter of limited government.
clues: English barons forced a king to seal this agreement in 1215.
It established that even the monarch was subject to the law of the land.
Its Clause 39 inspired the due process guarantees in the U.S. Constitution.
explanation: Sealed by King John in 1215, Magna Carta established rule-of-law limits on royal power and influenced due process.

trap_notes.a: The English Bill of Rights was enacted in 1689 after the Glorious Revolution.
trap_notes.c: The Mayflower Compact was signed by Pilgrims in Massachusetts in 1620.
trap_notes.d: The Peace of Westphalia ended the Thirty Years' War in 1648.
trap_notes.default: Magna Carta (1215) is the medieval charter that anchored due process and rule of law.

prompt: Identify this early colonial self-government agreement.
clues: Male passengers signed this brief pledge aboard a ship in November 1620.
Signers agreed to form a civil body politic and obey just, equal laws.
It is celebrated as an early North American example of social-contract consent.
explanation: Signed in 1620 before landing at Plymouth, the Mayflower Compact bound settlers to majority self-rule.

trap_notes.a: George Mason drafted the Virginia Declaration of Rights in 1776.
trap_notes.b: The Articles of Confederation were drafted by the Continental Congress in 1777.
trap_notes.d: The Northwest Ordinance was passed by Congress in 1787.
trap_notes.default: The 1620 Mayflower Compact established self-government by consent in Plymouth Colony.

prompt: Identify this Article I legislative rule.
clues: This Article I, Section 7 clause governs how federal tax laws begin.
It gives the chamber closest to voters the sole power to start revenue bills.
The Senate may still propose amendments to these bills after receiving them.
explanation: The Origination Clause requires all bills for raising revenue to originate in the House of Representatives.

trap_notes.b: The Supremacy Clause in Article VI makes federal law supreme over state law.
trap_notes.c: The Establishment Clause in the First Amendment bars government-established religion.
trap_notes.d: The Free Exercise Clause in the First Amendment protects religious practice.
trap_notes.default: The Origination Clause ensures tax bills begin in the directly elected House.

prompt: Identify this Reconstruction-era constitutional amendment.
clues: Ratified in December 1865, it was the first of three Reconstruction amendments.
It abolished slavery and involuntary servitude across the entire United States.
It retains a narrow exception allowing forced labor as punishment for a crime.
explanation: The Thirteenth Amendment (1865) permanently abolished slavery nationwide, extending beyond the Emancipation Proclamation.

trap_notes.a: The Twelfth Amendment (1804) reformed Electoral College balloting.
trap_notes.c: The Seventeenth Amendment (1913) established direct election of senators.
trap_notes.d: The Nineteenth Amendment (1920) guaranteed women's right to vote.
trap_notes.default: Ratified in 1865, the Thirteenth Amendment outlawed slavery throughout the United States.

prompt: Identify this Progressive-era constitutional amendment.
clues: Ratified in February 1913, it overturned an 1895 Supreme Court tax ruling.
It expanded federal fiscal capacity without apportioning taxes by state population.
It explicitly authorized Congress to lay and collect taxes on incomes.
explanation: The Sixteenth Amendment (1913) gave Congress clear power to levy a federal income tax.

trap_notes.a: The Eleventh Amendment (1795) limits federal lawsuits against states.
trap_notes.b: The Fourteenth Amendment (1868) established citizenship, due process, and equal protection.
trap_notes.d: The Twenty-first Amendment (1933) repealed national Prohibition.
trap_notes.default: The Sixteenth Amendment enabled the modern progressive federal income tax.

prompt: Identify this 1933 constitutional amendment.
clues: It is nicknamed the 'Lame Duck Amendment' because it shortened transition waits.
It moved the start of new congressional terms from March 4 to January 3.
It also set January 20 as the inauguration date for the president and vice president.
explanation: Ratified in 1933, the Twentieth Amendment reduced the lame-duck period by moving inaugurations to January.

trap_notes.a: The Eighteenth Amendment (1919) enacted Prohibition.
trap_notes.c: The Twenty-second Amendment (1951) limited presidents to two elected terms.
trap_notes.d: The Twenty-fifth Amendment (1967) clarified presidential succession and disability.
trap_notes.default: The Twentieth Amendment moved federal terms from March to January.

prompt: Identify this voting-rights constitutional amendment.
clues: Ratified in 1961, it changed presidential elections without creating a new state.
It granted federal district residents their first voice in choosing a president.
It awards Washington, D.C. electors equal to the least populous state, capped at three.
explanation: The Twenty-third Amendment (1961) gave Washington, D.C. three Electoral College votes in presidential races.

trap_notes.b: The Twenty-fourth Amendment (1964) banned poll taxes in federal elections.
trap_notes.c: The Twenty-sixth Amendment (1971) lowered the voting age to eighteen.
trap_notes.d: The Twenty-seventh Amendment (1992) delayed congressional pay raises.
trap_notes.default: The Twenty-third Amendment granted D.C. residents presidential electors.

prompt: Identify this core judicial power.
clues: This authority is not explicitly named in the text of Article III.
Alexander Hamilton defended it in Federalist No. 78 as essential to limited government.
It empowers courts to strike down laws or executive acts that violate the Constitution.
explanation: Established in Marbury v. Madison (1803), judicial review lets courts invalidate unconstitutional laws.

trap_notes.a: Executive privilege protects confidential presidential communications.
trap_notes.b: Senatorial courtesy gives home-state senators influence over judicial nominees.
trap_notes.c: Legislative oversight is Congress's monitoring of executive agencies.
trap_notes.default: Judicial review is the courts' power to measure laws against the Constitution.

prompt: Identify this implied presidential doctrine.
clues: Presidents invoke this doctrine to withhold certain records from Congress or courts.
It rests on the idea that candid advice to the president requires confidentiality.
The Supreme Court ruled in 1974 that it is qualified, not absolute, in criminal trials.
explanation: Executive privilege shields sensitive executive communications, though United States v. Nixon limited it.

trap_notes.b: A pocket veto occurs when the president leaves a bill unsigned as Congress adjourns.
trap_notes.c: A signing statement is a written comment issued when signing a bill into law.
trap_notes.d: Sovereign immunity bars lawsuits against the government without its consent.
trap_notes.default: Executive privilege protects confidential presidential advice unless outweighed by justice.

prompt: Identify this presidential legislative action.
clues: It occurs without the president writing a veto message or returning the bill.
It can only happen during the ten-day window right after Congress adjourns.
Because Congress is no longer in session, lawmakers cannot vote to override it.
explanation: A pocket veto kills a bill when the president does not sign it and Congress adjourns within ten days.

trap_notes.a: A discharge petition is a House tool to bring a bill out of committee.
trap_notes.c: A cloture vote ends a filibuster in the U.S. Senate.
trap_notes.d: An executive order directs federal agencies without legislative passage.
trap_notes.default: Unlike a regular veto, a pocket veto cannot be overridden by Congress.

prompt: Identify this powerful congressional committee.
clues: Established in 1789, it is the oldest standing committee in the U.S. House.
Its jurisdiction covers tariffs, Social Security, Medicare, and federal taxes.
Under the Origination Clause, all revenue bills begin under its authority.

explanation: The House Ways and Means Committee is the chief tax-writing panel in the U.S. Congress.

trap_notes.a: The Senate Judiciary Committee reviews federal judicial nominations and criminal law.
trap_notes.b: The House Rules Committee sets floor debate terms rather than writing tax bills.
trap_notes.d: The Senate Foreign Relations Committee handles treaties and diplomatic nominees.
trap_notes.default: House Ways and Means writes federal tax, tariff, and entitlement legislation.

prompt: Identify this federal budget stopgap measure.
clues: Congress passes this temporary bill when annual spending bills miss the deadline.
It keeps federal agencies operating at existing funding levels for weeks or months.
Without it or full appropriations, a federal government shutdown begins.
explanation: A continuing resolution extends prior-year federal funding temporarily while Congress finishes full budgets.

trap_notes.b: A conference report is the final compromise text of any bill from both chambers.
trap_notes.c: A line-item veto was struck down by the Supreme Court in 1998.
trap_notes.d: A discharge motion pulls a stalled bill out of a House committee.
trap_notes.default: Continuing resolutions prevent government shutdowns when appropriations lapse.

prompt: Identify this type of federal grant to states.
clues: Congress sends these funds to states or cities for a narrowly defined purpose.
Recipients must follow strict federal rules and often provide matching funds.
Examples include Medicaid and school lunch subsidies, unlike broad block grants.
explanation: Categorical grants give states federal money for specific programs with strict federal conditions.

trap_notes.a: Unfunded mandates require state action without providing federal money.
trap_notes.c: Interstate compacts are formal agreements between two or more states.
trap_notes.d: Property tax rebates are state or local tax credits, not federal grants.
trap_notes.default: Categorical grants restrict how states spend federal funds, unlike flexible block grants.

prompt: Identify this legal doctrine governing local governments.
clues: Named for an Iowa judge in 1868, it defines the status of cities and counties.
It holds that municipalities are creatures of the state, not independent sovereigns.
Under this rule, local governments exercise only powers expressly granted by the state.
explanation: Dillon's Rule limits municipal authority to powers expressly granted or implied by state law.

trap_notes.b: Incorporation applies the Bill of Rights to states via the Fourteenth Amendment.
trap_notes.c: Nullification was a rejected claim that states could void federal laws.
trap_notes.d: Senatorial courtesy concerns federal judicial nominations.
trap_notes.default: Dillon's Rule contrasts with home rule by narrowly construing city powers.

prompt: Identify this landmark 1896 Supreme Court ruling.
clues: The case began when a Louisiana man challenged a segregated railway car law.
Only Justice John Marshall Harlan dissented, writing that our Constitution is color-blind.
The majority upheld Jim Crow segregation under the 'separate but equal' doctrine.
explanation: Plessy v. Ferguson (1896) legitimized racial segregation until Brown v. Board overturned it in 1954.

trap_notes.a: Dred Scott v. Sandford (1857) denied citizenship to enslaved and free Black people.
trap_notes.c: Korematsu v. United States (1944) upheld wartime Japanese American internment.
trap_notes.d: Loving v. Virginia (1967) struck down state bans on interracial marriage.
trap_notes.default: Plessy v. Ferguson created the separate-but-equal precedent for Jim Crow laws.

prompt: Identify this World War II Supreme Court decision.
clues: A California citizen challenged Executive Order 9066 during World War II.
The 1944 majority upheld forced exclusion of Japanese Americans as a military necessity.
The Supreme Court formally repudiated this ruling in 2018 as gravely wrong.
explanation: Korematsu v. United States (1944) upheld wartime internment exclusion orders, though later widely condemned.

trap_notes.a: Schenck v. United States (1919) involved World War I anti-draft pamphlets.
trap_notes.b: Ex parte Milligan (1866) barred military trials of civilians where civil courts operated.
trap_notes.d: Youngstown (1952) barred President Truman from seizing steel mills.
trap_notes.default: Korematsu upheld Japanese American wartime exclusion before being repudiated in 2018.

prompt: Identify this 1967 civil rights Supreme Court case.
clues: An interracial couple was sentenced to prison under a Virginia felony statute.
Chief Justice Earl Warren wrote for a unanimous Court in June 1967.
The ruling struck down all remaining state bans on interracial marriage.
explanation: Loving v. Virginia (1967) held that anti-miscegenation laws violate Equal Protection and Due Process.

trap_notes.b: Gideon v. Wainwright (1963) guaranteed defense lawyers for indigent felony defendants.
trap_notes.c: Mapp v. Ohio (1961) applied the exclusionary rule to state courts.
trap_notes.d: Obergefell v. Hodges (2015) recognized same-sex marriage nationwide.
trap_notes.default: Loving v. Virginia invalidated state laws banning interracial marriage.

prompt: Identify this landmark 1969 First Amendment case.
clues: It replaced the older 'clear and present danger' standard for punishing speech.

Speech loses protection only if it incites imminent lawless action likely to occur.

trap_notes.c: Texas v. Johnson (1989) protected political flag burning.
trap_notes.d: Hazelwood v. Kuhlmeier (1988) allowed school oversight of student newspapers.
trap_notes.default: Brandenburg v. Ohio set the modern First Amendment test for incitement.

prompt: Identify this 2008 Second Amendment Supreme Court case.
clues: A special police officer challenged a strict handgun ban in the nation's capital.

trap_notes.c: Shelby County v. Holder (2013) invalidated the Voting Rights Act coverage formula.

prompt: Identify this 2015 Fourteenth Amendment Supreme Court case.
clues: Plaintiffs from Ohio, Michigan, Kentucky, and Tennessee challenged state marriage bans.

explanation: Obergefell v. Hodges (2015) guaranteed the fundamental right to marry for same-sex couples nationwide.

trap_notes.b: Loving v. Virginia (1967) struck down bans on interracial marriage.
trap_notes.c: Baker v. Carr (1962) allowed federal courts to review malapportioned districts.
trap_notes.d: Wisconsin v. Yoder (1972) protected Amish religious exemptions from high school.
trap_notes.default: Obergefell v. Hodges legalized same-sex marriage across all fifty states.

prompt: Identify this landmark 1965 federal statute.
clues: Passed after the Selma-to-Montgomery marches, it enforced the Fifteenth Amendment.

trap_notes.a: The Civil Rights Act of 1964 targeted public accommodations and employment discrimination.
trap_notes.c: The Fair Housing Act of 1968 barred discrimination in housing sales and rentals.

prompt: Identify this First Amendment press doctrine.
clues: It happens when officials try to block speech or news before it is published.

explanation: Prior restraint is government censorship before publication, which carries a heavy presumption of invalidity.

trap_notes.a: Strict scrutiny is a judicial standard of review, not pre-publication censorship.
trap_notes.b: Actual malice is the standard public officials must prove in libel lawsuits.
trap_notes.d: Symbolic speech refers to expressive conduct like wearing armbands.
trap_notes.default: Prior restraint blocks publication in advance rather than punishing unlawful speech afterward.

prompt: Identify this Fifth Amendment criminal-justice protection.
clues: This safeguard prevents prosecutors from retrying a defendant after an acquittal.

Under dual sovereignty, however, both state and federal courts may prosecute separately.
explanation: The Double Jeopardy Clause bars being tried or punished twice for the same offense by the same sovereign.

trap_notes.a: The exclusionary rule bars illegally seized evidence under the Fourth Amendment.
trap_notes.c: Eminent domain allows government to take private property for public use with just pay.
trap_notes.d: Habeas corpus challenges unlawful detention before a judge.
trap_notes.default: Double jeopardy protects acquitted defendants from repeated prosecutions by the same government.

prompt: Identify this redistricting practice.
clues: Its name comes from an 1812 Massachusetts governor and a salamander-shaped map.
Mapmakers use tactics called 'packing' and 'cracking' to dilute rival voters.
It manipulates legislative district borders to favor one party or incumbent.
explanation: Gerrymandering draws bizarrely shaped or partisan districts to maximize one party's legislative seats.

trap_notes.a: Malapportionment occurs when districts have unequal populations.
trap_notes.b: Logrolling is lawmakers trading votes on different bills.
trap_notes.d: Filibustering is using prolonged debate to stall a bill in the Senate.

prompt: Identify this party nominating contest.
clues: Voters cast secret ballots to select a party's nominee for the general election.
Unlike a closed contest, voters do not need prior party registration to take part.
On election day, any registered voter may choose which single party ballot to use.
explanation: In an open primary, any registered voter can pick one party's primary ballot without pre-registering in that party.

trap_notes.a: A caucus is an in-person neighborhood meeting rather than a standard ballot primary.
trap_notes.b: A closed primary restricts participation to registered party members.
trap_notes.d: A runoff election is a second contest held when no candidate wins a majority.
trap_notes.default: Open primaries let independent and unaffiliated voters participate in party nominations.

prompt: Identify this campaign finance organization.

trap_notes.b: Traditional PACs face strict contribution caps and may donate directly to candidates.

trap_notes.d: Exploratory committees test whether a candidate should run for office.

prompt: Identify this interest-group advocacy strategy.

explanation: Grassroots lobbying rallies constituents to contact their elected officials directly on pending bills.

trap_notes.b: Amicus filings are legal briefs submitted to appellate courts.
trap_notes.c: Executive rulemaking is the process agencies use to issue federal regulations.
trap_notes.d: Horse-race reporting is media coverage focused on election polling.
trap_notes.default: Grassroots lobbying uses constituent pressure from the bottom up to sway lawmakers.

prompt: Identify this democratic system of government.
clues: Voters elect the legislature, which then chooses the chief executive.
The head of government and cabinet sit inside the legislature, fusing both branches.
Canada, Japan, and the United Kingdom all operate under this constitutional model.
explanation: In a parliamentary democracy, the prime minister and cabinet emerge from and remain accountable to the legislature.

trap_notes.a: Presidential republics separate executive and legislative elections.
trap_notes.c: Absolute monarchies concentrate unchecked power in a hereditary ruler.
trap_notes.d: Confederations are weak alliances of sovereign states.
trap_notes.default: Parliamentary systems fuse executive and legislative authority through a prime minister.

prompt: Identify this regional supranational union.
clues: It grew out of 1950s coal, steel, and common market agreements in Western Europe.

Its institutions include a directly elected Parliament in Strasbourg and a Commission.

trap_notes.a: The African Union unites 55 African states and is headquartered in Addis Ababa.
trap_notes.c: The WTO is a global trade organization based in Geneva.
trap_notes.d: NATO is a transatlantic military defense alliance.
trap_notes.default: The European Union is the world's most deeply integrated supranational organization.

prompt: Identify this body of international humanitarian law.
clues: First drafted in 1864 and updated in four treaties in 1949, it governs armed conflict.
It sets binding rules for humane treatment of wounded soldiers, medics, and prisoners.
Its Fourth Convention specifically protects civilians in war zones and occupied lands.
explanation: The 1949 Geneva Conventions form the core of international humanitarian law protecting war victims and civilians.

trap_notes.b: The 1944 Bretton Woods Accords created the IMF and World Bank.
trap_notes.c: The 1997 Kyoto Protocol addressed greenhouse-gas emissions.
trap_notes.d: The 1823 Monroe Doctrine was a U.S. foreign-policy statement on the Americas.
trap_notes.default: The Geneva Conventions establish legal protections for prisoners, medics, and civilians in war.

explanation: In single-member districts, a party with 12% spread thinly across districts can win zero seats, favoring two parties.

trap_notes.c: The Red Party won 42 seats, short of a 51-seat majority.
trap_notes.d: The Blue Party won 58 seats, a clear majority.

prompt: Based on the table, which statement distinguishes a parliamentary system from a presidential one?

options.text: The chief executive serves a fixed term regardless of legislative votes
The head of state and chief executive are always the same person
The chief executive is chosen by the legislature and needs its confidence
Voters elect the prime minister on a separate national ballot

trap_notes.b: Combining head of state and head of government is a presidential feature.
trap_notes.d: Separately electing the chief executive describes a presidential system.

Both unitary and federal systems equally

trap_notes.d: Unitary and federal systems differ sharply on whether subnational units have protected powers.

prompt: What pattern does the table reveal about term length and minimum age across federal offices?

prompt: According to the table, what is required to remove an impeached official from office?

stimulus.title: Criminal Justice Protections in the Bill of Rights
